mainEntity.name: What is method overloading in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Method overloading in Java is a feature that allows a class to have multiple methods with the same name, provided they differ in their parameter list — either in the number of parameters, the types of parameters, or the order of parameter types. The compiler determines which version to call at compile time based on the arguments supplied at the call site. This is also called compile-time polymorphism or static polymorphism. Return type alone is NOT sufficient to overload a method in Java.

mainEntity.name: What are the rules for method overloading in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rules for method overloading in Java: (1) The method name must be the same. (2) The parameter list must be different — different number, different types, or different order of types. (3) Return type can be the same or different, but return type ALONE cannot distinguish overloaded methods. (4) Access modifiers and exceptions can also differ. (5) Overloading is resolved at compile time (static dispatch). (6) Overloading can happen within the same class or in a subclass (though in a subclass, changing only the return type of an inherited method creates a compile error).

mainEntity.name: What is type promotion in method overloading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Type promotion (also called implicit widening conversion) occurs during overload resolution when there is no exact match for the argument type. Java automatically widens the argument to the next compatible type to find a matching overload. The promotion chain for numeric types is: byte → short → int → long → float → double. For example, if you call add(5) and only add(long x) exists (not add(int x)), Java promotes 5 (int) to long and calls add(long). char can be promoted to int and then further up the chain. Widening always takes priority over autoboxing in overload resolution.

mainEntity.name: Can we overload the main method in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the main method can be overloaded in Java. You can define multiple methods named 'main' with different parameter lists: public static void main(String[] args), public static void main(int x), public static void main(String msg), etc. However, the JVM only uses the specific 'public static void main(String[] args)' signature as the program entry point. The other overloaded versions are treated as regular methods and must be called explicitly from code — the JVM will not invoke them automatically at startup.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Method overloading: same method name, different parameter list, within the same class (or subclass). Resolved at compile time (static polymorphism). Return type, access modifier, and exceptions can vary. Method overriding: same method name, same parameter list, same return type (or covariant), in a subclass overriding an inherited method. Resolved at runtime (dynamic polymorphism). Access modifier cannot be more restrictive; checked exceptions cannot be broader. Overloading is about providing multiple versions of a method for different input types; overriding is about replacing a parent class's behavior in a child class.

sections.title: What is Method Overloading in Java?

blocks.text: Method overloading in Java is the ability to define multiple methods with the same name in the same class, as long as their parameter lists are different. The Java compiler selects the correct version of the method at compile time based on the number, types, and order of the arguments passed — making it a form of compile-time polymorphism (also called static polymorphism or ad hoc polymorphism).

Without overloading, you would need different method names for logically identical operations on different data types — addInt(int, int), addDouble(double, double), addLong(long, long). Overloading lets all three simply be called add(), making the API cleaner and more intuitive. In real applications, overloading is everywhere: System.out.println() has 10 overloaded versions, String.valueOf() has 9, and Math.max() has 4.

Overloading is resolved entirely at compile time — the JVM does not make any runtime decision about which overload to invoke. This makes overloaded method calls as efficient as direct method calls. It is completely different from method overriding, which involves runtime dispatch and inheritance.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Method Overloading at a Glance
blocks.text: Key facts: (1) Same method name, different parameter list — that is the entire definition. (2) Can differ by: number of parameters, type of parameters, or order of parameter types. (3) Return type ALONE cannot distinguish overloads — it causes a compile error. (4) Resolved at compile time — no runtime overhead. (5) Also applies to constructors (constructor overloading). (6) Type promotion (widening) is applied automatically when there is no exact match. (7) Varargs overloads are chosen last — only when no non-varargs overload matches.

sections.title: Rules of Method Overloading — What the Compiler Checks

blocks.text: The Java compiler enforces a precise set of rules to determine whether two methods constitute valid overloads or a duplicate definition error. Understanding these rules prevents compile errors and unexpected resolution behavior.

items.title: Rule 1 — Same Method Name
items.text: Overloaded methods MUST share the exact same name (case-sensitive). 'print' and 'Print' are different methods, not overloads. The same name is the entire point of overloading — providing multiple implementations under one intuitive name.

items.title: Rule 2 — Different Parameter List
items.text: The parameter list must differ in at least one of: (a) Number of parameters — add(int) vs add(int, int). (b) Type of parameters — add(int, int) vs add(double, double). (c) Order of parameter types — display(String, int) vs display(int, String). Parameter NAMES do not matter — display(int a, String b) and display(int x, String y) are the same signature.

items.title: Rule 3 — Return Type Alone Is NOT Enough
items.text: Two methods with the same name and same parameter list but different return types cause a COMPILE ERROR — they are not valid overloads. Java cannot distinguish them from the call site alone: 'add(1,2)' gives no information about which return type is expected. This is a fundamental rule: return type never participates in overload resolution.

items.title: Rule 4 — Access Modifier & Exceptions Can Vary
items.text: Overloaded methods can have different access modifiers (public, private, protected, package-private) and different throws clauses. These do not affect overload resolution — the compiler selects the overload purely from the parameter list, then applies the access check.

items.title: Rule 5 — Can Exist in Same Class or Subclass
items.text: Overloaded methods can be defined in the same class. A subclass can also add overloads to an inherited method by defining a method with the same name but a different parameter list. This is still overloading (not overriding), resolved at compile time.

items.title: Rule 6 — Static Methods Can Be Overloaded
items.text: Static methods follow the same overloading rules as instance methods. Math.min(int,int), Math.min(long,long), Math.min(float,float), Math.min(double,double) are all static overloads. Overloading is independent of whether methods are static or instance.

blocks.text: The simplest and most readable form of overloading: defining the same method for different numbers of arguments. This is the Java idiom for default parameter values — since Java has no built-in default arguments (unlike Python or Kotlin), overloading is how you provide optional parameters cleanly.

blocks.title: 💡 The Delegation Pattern for Overloads
blocks.text: When overloading by parameter count, have shorter overloads DELEGATE to the longest (most complete) version by supplying default values. This avoids code duplication: the actual logic lives in exactly one place. If the logic changes, you update one method. This is the standard Java pattern for optional parameters — used throughout the JDK in classes like PrintStream, String, and Collections.

Overloading by parameter type is the most common form — providing type-specific implementations under a single method name. This is how the Java standard library achieves a clean API: Math.abs(int), Math.abs(long), Math.abs(float), Math.abs(double) all share one name and the compiler picks the right version automatically.

While valid, it often leads to confusing call sites where the caller must know the order to determine which version runs. It should be used only when the order genuinely conveys different semantic meaning.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Order-Based Overloading Is Often a Design Smell
blocks.text: Overloading by parameter order only works when the parameter types are DIFFERENT (e.g., String and int). Two methods with the same types in different order but same names are a valid overload — but at the call site, log("msg", 404) and log(404, "msg") look nearly identical and are easy to mix up. Prefer clearly named, distinct methods or a parameter object over order-based overloads in production code.

When the compiler cannot find an exact type match for a method call, it applies automatic type promotion (widening conversion) to find the closest compatible overload. The promotion chain for numeric primitives is: byte → short → int → long → float → double. A char is first promoted to int and then follows the chain. This happens silently at compile time — the programmer may not realize which overload is actually called.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Overload Resolution Priority Order
blocks.text: When Java resolves an overloaded call, it tries in this order: (1) Exact type match — highest priority. (2) Widening (type promotion) — next. (3) Autoboxing/unboxing — e.g., int → Integer. (4) Varargs — lowest priority, only chosen when nothing else matches. If multiple promotions are equally valid, the compiler reports an ambiguity error. Knowing this order is critical for predicting which overload runs.

sections.title: Return Type & Overloading — Why Return Type Alone Fails

blocks.text: A fundamental rule in Java: return type alone cannot distinguish overloaded methods. If two methods have the same name and the same parameter list but different return types, the compiler reports a duplicate method error — not a valid overload. This is because at the call site, the compiler determines which overload to invoke before it knows what return type the caller expects.

blocks.label: ReturnTypeOverloading.java
lines: // ❌ INVALID — only return type differs, same parameter list → COMPILE ERROR
// public int    convert(String s) { return Integer.parseInt(s); }
// public double convert(String s) { return Double.parseDouble(s); } // ERROR
// convert("42")  — compiler cannot tell which return type you want
// Even: int x = convert("42") — this is checked AFTER overload resolution
public static int    convertToInt(String s)    { return Integer.parseInt(s); }
public static double convertToDouble(String s) { return Double.parseDouble(s); }
// ✅ Fix: Use different parameter types (then return type can differ too)
public static int    parse(String s) { return Integer.parseInt(s); }
public static double parse(String s, boolean asDecimal) {
return Double.parseDouble(s); // Now parameter list differs — valid overload
// ✅ VALID: Same name, different params — return types CAN differ when params differ
public static int    getValue(int index)    { return index * 10; }
public static String getValue(String key)   { return "Value of " + key; }
public static double getValue(double ratio) { return ratio * 100; }
// Compiler uses parameter type to resolve — return types are fine here

blocks.title: 📌 Covariant Return Types — Overriding, Not Overloading
blocks.text: While return type cannot distinguish overloads, Java DOES allow a subclass to narrow (covariant) the return type when OVERRIDING: if the parent declares 'Animal create()', the child can declare 'Dog create()' — Dog is a subtype of Animal. This is covariant return type and applies only to overriding (runtime polymorphism), not overloading (compile-time polymorphism).

sections.title: Varargs and Method Overloading — The Last Resort

blocks.text: Varargs (type...) can be used in overloaded methods, but they interact with overload resolution in a specific and sometimes surprising way. The Java compiler treats a varargs overload as the last resort — it is chosen only when no non-varargs overload matches the call. This makes varargs a natural 'catch-all' fallback while specific overloads handle common cases efficiently.

blocks.label: VarargsOverloading.java
lines: // Specific overloads for 1 and 2 args (most common cases — no array overhead)
public static int sum(int a, int b) {
// Non-varargs preferred over varargs when both match
print("hello");  // String version chosen (more specific than Object...)
print(1, 2);     // varargs Object version (no String overload for 2 args)
// Two varargs overloads that can both match a specific call:
// sum(int... nums) and sum(Integer... nums) — calling sum(1,2) is ambiguous

blocks.title: ⚠️ Varargs Overloading Ambiguity — The Compiler Cannot Choose
blocks.text: Never define two overloads where both are varargs and both could match the same call: 'void show(int... nums)' and 'void show(Integer... nums)' — calling show(1, 2) causes an ambiguity compile error because 1 can be either int or Integer. Similarly, 'void show(Object... o)' and 'void show(String... s)' can conflict. Rule: if you have a varargs overload, ensure it cannot collide with other varargs overloads for the same argument types.

sections.title: Constructor Overloading — Multiple Ways to Build an Object

blocks.text: Constructor overloading applies the same principle — multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists. This allows objects to be created in multiple ways: with all fields, with some fields (others defaulting), or from different data sources. The this() call allows one constructor to delegate to another, avoiding code duplication — the same delegation pattern used with method overloads.

return name + " | " + department + " | ₹" + salary + " | active=" + isActive;
// ✅ this() must be the FIRST statement in a constructor
// ❌ Cannot call both this() and super() in same constructor

blocks.title: 💡 this() Must Be the First Statement
blocks.text: When using this() to delegate to another constructor, it MUST be the very first statement in the constructor body. You cannot execute any other statements before this(). Also, you cannot use both this() and super() in the same constructor — they are mutually exclusive. The delegation chain must terminate at a constructor that does NOT call this() — that one performs the actual initialization.

sections.title: Overloading vs Overriding — The Most Important Distinction

blocks.text: Method overloading and method overriding are both forms of polymorphism in Java, but they are fundamentally different mechanisms. Overloading is resolved at compile time (static polymorphism). Overriding is resolved at runtime (dynamic polymorphism). Confusing the two is among the most common mistakes in Java interviews and code.

sections.title: Compile-Time Polymorphism — How the JVM Resolves Overloads

blocks.text: Method overloading is also called compile-time polymorphism or static polymorphism because the binding between a method call and its implementation is resolved during compilation, not at runtime. The Java compiler analyzes the argument types at the call site, applies the overload resolution rules, and emits a direct invokestatic or invokevirtual bytecode instruction pointing to the specific overload. No runtime dispatch table lookup is needed.

blocks.label: CompileTimePolymorphism.java
lines: // Compile time: compiler sees literal 42 → int → picks print(int)
// Compile time: compiler sees literal "Hello" → String → picks print(String)
// Compile time: compiler sees literal 3.14 → double → picks print(double)
// ⚠️ Reference type vs actual type — overloading uses REFERENCE type!
// This is different from overriding which uses ACTUAL (runtime) type
p.print(obj.toString()); // print(String) — called via explicit toString()
// Key insight: if print(Object obj) existed:
// p.print(obj) would call print(Object) — because obj's DECLARED type is Object
// NOT print(String) — even though obj holds a String at runtime
// Overloading binds at compile time using DECLARED type, not runtime type

blocks.title: ⚠️ Critical: Overloading Uses Declared (Static) Type — Not Runtime Type
blocks.text: Unlike overriding (which uses the actual runtime type), overloading resolution uses the DECLARED (compile-time) type of the reference. If Object obj = "Hello" and you call show(obj), Java calls show(Object) — NOT show(String) — even though obj holds a String at runtime. This surprises many developers. Rule: overload resolution is 100% a compile-time decision based on the declared types of the arguments, ignoring what those references actually point to at runtime.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These mistakes appear consistently in beginner and even intermediate Java code. Each one compiles without error or warning but produces wrong or unexpected behavior at runtime.

blocks.label: OverloadingMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Assuming return type differentiates overloads
// public String getData() { return "one"; } // COMPILE ERROR — not an overload
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Assuming parameter names differentiate overloads
// public void process(int code) { } // COMPILE ERROR — same signature
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Unexpected type promotion picks wrong overload

// Developer expected int or double — gets long via promotion
// Fix: add an int overload, or explicitly cast: show((double)i)
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Overloading with declared type vs runtime type
// Overloading is resolved at COMPILE TIME using DECLARED type
// If show(Object x) and show(String x) both existed:
// Because obj is declared as Object, not String
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: null argument — ambiguity between reference-type overloads

// find(null) → COMPILE ERROR: ambiguous, both String and Integer accept null
// Fix: cast explicitly: find((String) null) or find((Integer) null)

// check(5) → autoboxes 5 to Integer and calls check(Integer)

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These overloading anti-patterns are common reasons for failed code reviews and maintenance headaches in professional Java teams. Each one abuses overloading in ways that reduce clarity or cause subtle bugs.

items.title: Overloading with Inconsistent Semantics
items.text: All overloads of a method MUST do the same logical operation on different types or argument counts. 'void process(int id)' that fetches a user and 'void process(String command)' that executes a shell command — same name, completely different behavior. This destroys the principle of least surprise. Rename them: fetchUser(int id) and executeCommand(String cmd).

items.title: Too Many Overloads (Overload Explosion)
items.text: Defining 6, 7, 8+ overloads of the same method for every possible combination of optional parameters creates an explosion of methods. Readers must scan all overloads to understand the API. Use the Builder pattern or a parameter object (record) instead. A good rule: if you have more than 4 overloads of the same method, consider a builder.

items.title: Overloading Based on Order of Same Types
items.text: Having both 'void register(String firstName, String lastName)' and 'void register(String lastName, String firstName)' is a disaster — both have the same signature! This won't even compile (both are String, String). Even if the types differ slightly, order-only overloads confuse callers and are trivial to call incorrectly. Use a named object: register(PersonName name).

items.title: Mixing Varargs and Specific Overloads Carelessly
items.text: Adding a varargs overload to a class that already has many specific overloads can cause unexpected resolution. If 'print(String)' exists and you add 'print(Object... objs)', calling print("hello") works — but print((Object)"hello") now goes to varargs. Callers cannot easily predict which version runs without checking the resolution rules.

items.title: Overloading Purely for Auto-Widening Side Effects
items.text: Designing overloads that intentionally exploit type promotion to route calls — e.g., leaving out an int overload so int calls auto-promote to long — is clever but fragile. A future developer adding an int overload changes the behavior of all existing int callers silently. Always provide the overload for the type you intend to handle rather than relying on promotion.

items.title: Not Using @Override When Intending to Override
items.text: If you intend to OVERRIDE a parent method but accidentally change the parameter type, Java silently treats it as an OVERLOAD — not an override. The parent method is not replaced; both exist. Using @Override forces the compiler to verify it's a true override. This is the most dangerous interaction between overloading and overriding — always use @Override on intended overrides.

blocks.label: OverloadingAntiPatterns.java
lines: // ❌ ANTI-PATTERN: Missing @Override — silently becomes overload instead of override
// ❌ Intended as override, but parameter type changed to String
// This is an OVERLOAD of save(), NOT an override — Base.save(Object) still exists
public void save(String data) {  // No @Override — compiler won't catch this
// Because overloading uses declared type (Base), and Base only has save(Object)
public void save(Object data) { // Compiler verifies this is a true override

sections.title: Java Method Overloading Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher interviews, OCPJP/OCA certification exams, and campus placement tests.

items.q: Q1. What is method overloading in Java? Why is it used?
items.a: Method overloading is defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists (different number, type, or order of parameters). It is used to: (1) Provide a clean, intuitive API — Math.max(int,int), Math.max(double,double) are all just 'max'. (2) Implement type-specific behavior under one name. (3) Simulate default parameter values — Java has no built-in default args, so shorter overloads delegate to longer ones with default values. (4) Reduce cognitive load — callers use one familiar name regardless of data type. It is resolved at compile time (static/compile-time polymorphism) — no runtime overhead.

items.q: Q2. Can we overload a method by changing only the return type?
items.a: No — this causes a COMPILE ERROR. Two methods with the same name and same parameter list but different return types are not valid overloads. The compiler determines which overload to call before it knows what return type the caller expects. For example, at 'int x = getData()', the call 'getData()' is resolved first — the compiler cannot use the left-hand side type to disambiguate. The fix is to either use different parameter lists or different method names.

items.q: Q3. What is the output? void show(int x){} void show(long x){} — which is called for show(5)?
items.a: show(int x) is called. The literal 5 is an int by default in Java. The compiler finds an exact match for int and calls show(int). No type promotion is needed. If show(int x) did NOT exist, then Java would promote 5 to long and call show(long). Type promotion only happens when there is no exact match — the compiler always prefers the most specific (narrowest) applicable overload.

items.q: Q4. What is type promotion in the context of method overloading?
items.a: Type promotion (widening conversion) is Java's automatic fallback when no exact-match overload exists for a given argument type. The compiler widens the argument to the next compatible type in the chain: byte → short → int → long → float → double. char is promoted to int first. Example: if only show(long x) and show(double x) exist, calling show(100) widens int 100 to long and calls show(long). Priority in overload resolution: (1) Exact match, (2) Widening/promotion, (3) Autoboxing, (4) Varargs.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
items.a: Overloading: same method name, different parameter list, same class. Resolved at COMPILE TIME (static polymorphism). Return type, access modifier, and exceptions can vary. No inheritance needed. Overriding: same method name, same parameter list, subclass replaces parent's implementation. Resolved at RUNTIME (dynamic polymorphism). Return type must be same or covariant. Access cannot be more restrictive. Requires @Override for safety. Key trick question: if you change the parameter type when 'overriding', you accidentally create an overload instead — the parent method is not replaced. Always use @Override to let the compiler catch this mistake.

items.q: Q6. Can we overload the main method in Java?
items.a: Yes. You can define multiple methods named 'main' with different parameter lists: public static void main(String[] args), public static void main(int x), public static void main(). They are all valid overloads and can be called explicitly from code. However, the JVM only recognizes 'public static void main(String[] args)' as the program entry point — no other overload is invoked automatically at startup. All other main overloads are treated as regular static methods.

items.q: Q7. What happens when null is passed to an overloaded method with multiple reference-type parameters?
items.a: If exactly one overload accepts a reference type compatible with null, that overload is called. Example: void find(String s) — find(null) calls it. If multiple overloads accept reference types (all compatible with null) and none is more specific, the compiler reports an AMBIGUITY ERROR: the call is ambiguous between find(String) and find(Integer). Fix: cast explicitly — find((String)null) or find((Integer)null). Rule: null is compatible with any reference type, so when multiple reference-type overloads exist, pass null with an explicit cast.

items.q: Q8. Does overloading work with static methods?
items.a: Yes. Static methods follow identical overloading rules. Math.min(int,int), Math.min(long,long), Math.min(float,float), Math.min(double,double) are four static overloads. Static methods CANNOT be overridden (a subclass defining the same static signature creates a separate hidden method, not an override), but they CAN be overloaded. Overloading is a compile-time, same-class feature and does not depend on the static/instance distinction.

items.q: Q9. How does autoboxing interact with method overloading?
items.a: Autoboxing (int → Integer, double → Double, etc.) participates in overload resolution, but has LOWER priority than widening. Priority: exact match > widening > autoboxing > varargs. So if show(int x) and show(Integer x) both exist: show(5) calls show(int) — exact match, no autoboxing. If only show(Integer x) exists: show(5) autoboxes 5 to Integer. If show(long x) and show(Integer x) both exist: show(5) prefers show(long) via widening over show(Integer) via autoboxing — widening is preferred. This surprises many developers: widening beats boxing.

items.q: Q10. What is the risk of overloading when combined with inheritance?
items.a: The main risk is accidentally creating an overload instead of an override. If parent has 'save(Object data)' and child defines 'save(String data)', the child has created an OVERLOAD — not an override. The parent's save(Object) still exists and is NOT replaced. When called through a parent reference: Animal a = new Dog(); a.save(obj) — this calls parent's save(Object) even if obj is a String, because overload resolution uses the DECLARED type (Animal) at compile time. The fix is always @Override, which forces the compiler to verify the signature matches exactly. This combination of overloading and polymorphism is one of the trickiest Java topics.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Overloading Knowledge

blocks.text: Challenge yourself with these practice questions. Attempt each independently before reading the answer — active recall is proven to be 2–3x more effective than passive reading.

items.a:
int: 10 — exact int match.
double: 10.0 — exact double match.
double: 10.0 — 10L is a long; no long overload exists, so it widens to double.
int: 5 — byte widens to int (nearest exact match in the chain). If int didn't exist, byte would promote to double.
Key: exact match wins always. When no exact match, nearest wider type in chain is chosen.

This does NOT compile. Error: 'compute(int, int)' is already defined. Two methods with the same name and same parameter list (int, int) differ only in return type — this is NOT valid overloading. Java cannot distinguish them at the call site compute(2,3) because return type is not used for overload resolution. Fix: either give them different names (computeSum, computeProduct) or use different parameter types.

display(obj) → prints 'Object' — obj is DECLARED as Object type. Overloading uses declared (compile-time) type, not runtime type. Even though obj holds a String at runtime, the compiler sees Object.
display("Hello") → prints 'String' — the literal "Hello" has declared type String. Exact String match is more specific than Object.
display(null) → prints 'String' — when multiple reference overloads exist and null is passed, Java picks the most specific type. String is more specific than Object (String IS-A Object), so String version wins. If both were equally specific (unrelated types), it would be ambiguous.

items.q: 4. Write an overloaded method 'format' that: (a) takes a double and returns it rounded to 2 decimal places as a String, (b) takes a double and an int (decimal places) and formats accordingly, (c) takes a String and an int (max length) and truncates if longer.

items.a: Output: 'long' — This demonstrates overload resolution priority: widening (int → long) is preferred over autoboxing (int → Integer). Even though Integer seems like the 'natural' box type for int, Java prefers the widening conversion to long because widening has higher priority than autoboxing in overload resolution. To call the Integer version, you must explicitly autobox: test(Integer.valueOf(i)) or test((Integer) i).

p.show("hello") → prints 'Parent Object' — NOT 'Child String'! Because overloading resolution uses the DECLARED type of p, which is Parent. Parent only has show(Object). So even though p holds a Child at runtime, the compiler sees Parent.show(Object) and calls that. The Child's show(String) is an OVERLOAD, not an override of Parent.show(Object).
p.show(new Object()) → prints 'Parent Object' — straightforward, only Parent.show(Object) matches.
To call Child's show(String), you need: ((Child)p).show("hello") — casting to Child exposes the String overload.

This causes a COMPILE ERROR: 'reference to go is ambiguous'. Both go(int,long) and go(long,int) are applicable when called with go(1, 2) — two int arguments. For go(int,long): first arg 1 is exact int, second arg 2 is promoted int→long. For go(long,int): first arg 1 is promoted int→long, second arg 2 is exact int. Both require exactly one widening promotion — neither is more specific than the other. Java cannot choose and reports ambiguity. Fix: provide an explicit go(int,int) overload, or cast at the call site: go(1, 2L) to force go(int,long).

sections.title: Conclusion — Method Overloading: Compile-Time Polymorphism Done Right

blocks.text: Method overloading is the foundation of clean, intuitive Java APIs. It allows a single logical operation to work across different data types and argument counts under one recognizable name — eliminating the need for type-encoded names like addInt, addDouble, or addWithDefault. The Java standard library is built on this principle: System.out.println, Math.max, String.valueOf are all overloaded for every type you'll ever need.

Mastering overloading means understanding not just the syntax, but the resolution rules: exact match first, then widening, then autoboxing, then varargs. It means knowing that declared type, not runtime type, governs overload selection. It means recognizing when overloading is the right tool (type-variant operations, optional parameters) versus when it introduces confusion (inconsistent semantics, too many overloads, order-based disambiguation).

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Method Overloading

items.q: What is method overloading in Java?
items.a: Method overloading is defining multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists — differing in number, type, or order of parameters. The compiler selects the correct version at compile time based on the arguments at the call site. It is also called compile-time polymorphism or static polymorphism. It makes APIs cleaner by allowing one intuitive method name to handle multiple types or argument counts.

items.q: What are the rules for method overloading in Java?
items.a: Rules: (1) Method name must be the same. (2) Parameter list must differ — in count, type, or order. (3) Return type alone cannot distinguish overloads. (4) Parameter names alone cannot distinguish overloads. (5) Access modifier, exceptions, and return type can all vary as long as the parameter list differs. (6) Overloading is resolved entirely at compile time using the declared types of the arguments.

items.q: What is type promotion in method overloading?
items.a: Type promotion (widening conversion) is Java's automatic fallback when no exact-type overload exists. The argument type is widened to the nearest compatible parameter type in the chain: byte→short→int→long→float→double. char promotes to int first. Java applies this silently — the developer may not realize which overload is selected. Overload resolution priority: exact match > widening > autoboxing > varargs.

items.q: Can we overload the main method in Java?
items.a: Yes. Multiple methods named 'main' with different parameter lists are valid overloads. Only 'public static void main(String[] args)' is recognized by the JVM as the program entry point. All other main overloads are regular methods and must be called explicitly from code — the JVM ignores them at startup.

items.q: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
items.a: Overloading: same name, different parameters, same class, resolved at compile time (static polymorphism). Overriding: same name, same parameters, subclass replaces parent's behavior, resolved at runtime (dynamic polymorphism). A critical trap: if you intend to override but accidentally change the parameter type, Java silently treats it as an overload — the parent's method is not replaced. Always use @Override to catch this mistake at compile time.
